question: A 6-year-old with a 4-month history of bilateral hearing loss undergoes tympanometry. Which finding is most consistent with otitis media with effusion?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A type A tympanogram indicates a normal, mobile tympanic membrane with normal middle ear pressure. OME causes reduced or absent compliance due to fluid filling the middle ear space.

answers.text: Type B tympanogram with normal ear canal volume

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Type B (flat) tympanogram with normal ear canal volume (0.6–1.2 mL) is the hallmark of OME — the flat curve indicates absent TM compliance due to fluid, and the normal canal volume confirms the drum is intact (distinguishing it from a perforation, which gives type B with a large canal volume).

answers.text: Type B tympanogram with a very large ear canal volume

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A type B tympanogram with very large canal volume (>2 mL in a child) indicates a tympanic membrane perforation or patent ventilation tube — the probe tip is effectively measuring the middle ear as part of the ear canal. This is not OME.

answers.text: Type C tympanogram with a peak at -200 daPa

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Partially related but not the best answer. A type C tympanogram indicates negative middle ear pressure (Eustachian tube dysfunction) without effusion. OME specifically is characterised by the flat type B curve, not a shifted type C peak.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: type B + normal canal volume = OME (fluid, intact drum); type B + large canal volume = perforation or patent grommet. Type C = Eustachian tube dysfunction without effusion.
Correct. Type B tympanogram with normal canal volume is the diagnostic signature of OME. The normal canal volume rules out perforation and confirms the TM is intact.
